title: Arenes
unit: A2 (unit number not stated in text; inferred from topic)

questions.question: Which organic compound reacts with a Grignard reagent to give a product that forms a secondary alcohol on hydrolysis? A carbon dioxide, B ethanal, C methanal, D propanone.
questions.answer: B ethanal
steps: A Grignard reagent adds to the C=O group of a carbonyl compound, giving an alkoxide that is hydrolysed to an alcohol.
Methanal gives a primary alcohol, and CO2 gives a carboxylic acid after hydrolysis.
Propanone (a ketone) gives a tertiary alcohol.
Ethanal (an aldehyde with one alkyl group on the carbonyl carbon) gives a secondary alcohol, so the answer is B.

questions.question: How many different amino acids were used to form the part of the protein structure shown in the PDF? A 3, B 4, C 5, D 6.
steps: Split the chain at each amide (peptide) link; each residue is N-CH(R)-C(=O) with side chain R on the alpha carbon.
Reading left to right the side chains are CH3 (alanine), H (glycine), CH2OH (serine), CH(OH)CH3 (threonine), CH2OH (serine), CH3 (alanine).
Alanine and serine each occur twice, so the different amino acids are alanine, glycine, serine and threonine = 4, option B.

questions.question: Using the standard enthalpies of combustion of cyclohexene and cyclohexa-1,4-diene (values in a table in the PDF), calculate the enthalpy of combustion of the theoretical compound cyclohexa-1,3,5-triene.
steps: Going from cyclohexene (-3752) to cyclohexa-1,4-diene (-3584) adds one C=C (loses H2): change = -3584 - (-3752) = +168 kJ mol^-1.
Adding the next C=C (cyclohexa-1,3,5-triene, C6H6) should change the value by the same +168 kJ mol^-1.
Triene = -3584 + 168 = -3416 kJ mol^-1 (compare benzene -3267, so benzene is about 149 kJ mol^-1 less exothermic, i.e. more stable).

questions.question: Explain the difference between the enthalpy of combustion of the theoretical cyclohexa-1,3,5-triene (calculated from localised C=C bonds) and the value for benzene given in the table.
questions.answer: The calculated triene value is more exothermic, because it has three localised C=C bonds; benzene is more stable (lower in energy) due to delocalisation, so it releases less energy on combustion
steps: The calculated value assumes three localised C=C double bonds, as in the Kekule structure.
Benzene has a delocalised ring of electrons, which lowers its energy and makes it more stable.
A more stable compound starts from a lower energy, so less energy is released when it burns.
The difference between the two values is the delocalisation (resonance) energy of benzene.

questions.question: Bromine reacts with cyclohexene to form 1,2-dibromocyclohexane and with benzene to form bromobenzene. Compare and contrast these reactions in terms of type, mechanism and conditions (mechanisms need not be drawn).
questions.answer: Cyclohexene undergoes electrophilic addition with bromine at room temperature without a catalyst, while benzene undergoes electrophilic substitution, requiring a halogen carrier such as AlBr3 or FeBr3 and retaining the ring
steps: Cyclohexene: electrophilic addition across the C=C; Br2 adds to give 1,2-dibromocyclohexane, with no catalyst at room temperature.
Benzene: electrophilic substitution, with H replaced by Br, giving bromobenzene and HBr.
Benzene needs a halogen carrier catalyst (AlBr3 or FeBr3) to polarise Br2 and make a strong enough electrophile.
Both involve an electrophile (Br+ from polarised Br2) attacking the pi electrons, but benzene's delocalised ring is stable, so substitution keeps the ring and addition is avoided.

questions.question: Identify the organic product when phenol reacts with excess bromine.
questions.answer: 2,4,6-tribromophenol (C6H2Br3OH)
steps: The -OH group activates the ring at positions 2, 4 and 6.
Excess bromine substitutes all three activated positions.
The product is 2,4,6-tribromophenol, which is a white precipitate.

questions.question: Explain why bromine reacts much faster with phenol than with benzene.
questions.answer: A lone pair on the oxygen of phenol is delocalised into the ring, increasing electron density on the ring, which makes it more attractive to the electrophile Br2 so no catalyst is needed
steps: The O atom in phenol has a lone pair that overlaps with the delocalised ring of electrons.
This donates electron density into the ring, making the ring more nucleophilic.
The electrophile Br2 is therefore attracted more strongly, so the reaction is faster.
No halogen carrier catalyst is needed, unlike benzene.

questions.question: Ethene reacts with bromine at room temperature, but benzene requires heat and a catalyst. Which best explains this? A delocalised electrons repel electrophiles, B they result in a kinetic barrier to intermediate formation, C benzene has an endothermic enthalpy of formation, D they make benzene thermodynamically stable with respect to bromobenzene.
questions.answer: B they result in a kinetic barrier to intermediate formation
steps: Benzene's stability comes from the delocalised ring, which must be disturbed for the reaction to proceed.
Attack by the electrophile produces a non-aromatic intermediate, which has a high activation energy.
This is a kinetic barrier, so heat and a catalyst are needed.
Option D describes thermodynamic stability, which does not explain why the reaction is slow, so B is the best answer.

questions.question: What is the product when benzene reacts with fuming sulfuric acid? The answer options are shown in the figure below.
questions.answer: D: benzenesulfonic acid, C6H5SO3H
steps: Fuming sulfuric acid contains SO3, which (or HSO3+) is the electrophile in electrophilic substitution of benzene.
One ring H is replaced by the sulfonic acid group -SO3H: sulfur is bonded to the ring, to two double-bonded oxygens (S=O) and to one -OH.
D shows exactly this group. A has no OH, B is a sulfinate (O-S bond to the ring, only one S=O), and C has only one S=O with two OH groups.

questions.question: Which of the given compounds could NOT be formed when excess benzene is heated with trichloromethane (CHCl3) in the presence of aluminium chloride? The options (structures) are shown in the figure below.
questions.answer: D: tetraphenylmethane, C(C6H5)4
steps: With AlCl3, CHCl3 acts as a Friedel-Crafts alkylating agent: each substitution replaces one C-Cl bond by a C-phenyl bond.
With excess benzene the products can be PhCHCl2 (A), Ph2CHCl (B) and Ph3CH (C, three phenyls, one H).
The C-H bond of CHCl3 is not substituted, so the carbon can never carry four phenyl groups; D cannot be formed.

questions.question: The delocalised electrons in benzene result from the overlap of which orbitals? Options A and B (s orbitals) and C and D (p orbitals) are given, differing in the bond symbol (Greek letter) shown in the figure below.
questions.answer: D: p orbitals overlapping sideways to form pi bonds
steps: Each carbon in benzene has one unhybridised p orbital perpendicular to the plane of the ring.
Sideways overlap of these p orbitals forms pi bonds, giving a ring of delocalised pi electrons above and below the plane.
s orbitals cannot give the delocalised system and sigma overlap is end-on, so only D is correct.

questions.question: Benzene is sometimes represented by a Kekule structure. If this were the only structure of benzene, how many isomers of dichlorobenzene would there be? A two, B three, C four, D five.
questions.answer: C four
steps: In the Kekule structure, the two Cl atoms in the ortho (1,2) position can be on a C=C double bond or on a C-C single bond, giving 2 ortho isomers.
The meta (1,3) and para (1,4) positions each give one isomer.
So the Kekule structure predicts 2 + 1 + 1 = 4 isomers.
Only three dichlorobenzene isomers are actually observed, which is evidence for the delocalised structure.

questions.question: What is the molar mass of the organic product when phenol reacts with excess bromine water? A 156.9, B 172.9, C 330.7, D 488.5 (g mol-1).
questions.answer: C 330.7 g mol-1
steps: Excess bromine water gives 2,4,6-tribromophenol, C6H2Br3OH (C6H3Br3O).
So the molar mass is 330.7 g mol-1, option C.

questions.topic: Sigma and Pi Bonds in Benzene
questions.question: How many sigma and how many pi bonds are there in a molecule of benzene? The answer options are shown in the figure below.
questions.answer: C: 12 sigma bonds and 3 pi bonds
steps: Sigma bonds: 6 C-C ring bonds + 6 C-H bonds = 12.
Pi bonds: each carbon contributes one p electron; the six electrons are equivalent to 3 pi bonds (delocalised over the ring).
So 12 sigma and 3 pi, option C.

questions.question: Compare and contrast the reactions of bromine with benzene and cyclohexene, and with benzene and phenol, considering the effects of delocalised electrons. Detailed bond or mechanism descriptions are not required.
questions.answer: Cyclohexene adds bromine readily with no catalyst; benzene resists addition because its delocalised ring is stable, so it needs a halogen carrier to substitute; phenol's oxygen lone pair is delocalised into the ring, activating it so it brominates without a catalyst
steps: Cyclohexene has a localised C=C bond, so bromine adds across it at room temperature with no catalyst, giving 1,2-dibromocyclohexane.
Benzene's delocalised electrons are stable, so addition would lose this stability and it does not happen easily.
Benzene needs a halogen carrier (AlBr3 or FeBr3) and heat, and undergoes substitution, keeping the delocalised ring.
Phenol's O lone pair is delocalised into the ring, increasing electron density on the ring, so it reacts with bromine water at room temperature with no catalyst.
Phenol gives 2,4,6-tribromophenol with excess bromine, whereas benzene gives monosubstitution under catalysed conditions.
So the delocalised electrons in benzene make it less reactive than cyclohexene, while in phenol the delocalised system is activated and more reactive than benzene.

questions.question: Benzene reacts with fuming sulfuric acid to form benzenesulfonic acid. Fuming sulfuric acid is: A sulfuric acid of 98 % concentration, B pure sulfuric acid, C concentrated sulfuric acid containing dissolved sulfur dioxide, D concentrated sulfuric acid containing dissolved sulfur trioxide.
questions.answer: D concentrated sulfuric acid containing dissolved sulfur trioxide
steps: Fuming sulfuric acid (oleum) is H2SO4 with excess SO3 dissolved in it.
The SO3 acts as the electrophile in sulfonation of benzene.
Sulfur dioxide and 98 % acid are not the source of the electrophile.
So option D is correct.

questions.question: Which is correct for the reaction of bromine with phenol when compared with benzene? The options are shown in the figure below.
questions.answer: A: phenol is more reactive, with a higher electron density in the ring
steps: A lone pair on the oxygen of phenol overlaps with the ring pi system and is partly delocalised into it.
This raises the electron density of the ring, so it polarises bromine more strongly and attacks it more readily.
Phenol is therefore more reactive than benzene (higher electron density), option A.

questions.question: Which statement explains why bromine reacts more readily with phenol than with benzene? A the O-H bond in phenol is polar, B the oxygen atom in phenol is very electronegative, C a lone pair of electrons on oxygen in phenol is delocalised into the ring, D the electron density in the ring is greater in benzene than in phenol.
questions.answer: C a lone pair of electrons on oxygen in phenol is delocalised into the ring
steps: The lone pair on the O atom of phenol overlaps with the ring's pi system.
This increases the electron density of the ring, which makes it more reactive towards electrophiles.
Options A and B describe features that do not explain the ring reactivity.
Option D is the reverse, since the ring of phenol has the higher electron density.

questions.question: What is the total number of delocalised electrons in anthracene? A 6, B 10, C 14, D 18.
steps: Anthracene (C14H10) has three fused benzene rings with 14 carbon atoms in the aromatic system.
Each carbon atom in the delocalised system contributes one p electron.
So there are 14 delocalised electrons, option C.

questions.question: Using the thermochemical, X-ray diffraction and bromination information on benzene and cyclohexene shown in the PDF, explain how this provides evidence that the electrons in the pi bonds of benzene are delocalised.
questions.answer: Benzene is more stable than a localised triene (hydrogenation), has six equal C-C bonds of intermediate length (X-ray) and reacts by substitution under harsher conditions than cyclohexene (bromination): all consistent with delocalised pi electrons.
steps: Thermochemical: cyclohexene -120 kJ mol^-1, so a Kekule benzene with three C=C would give 3 x -120 = -360 kJ mol^-1; the actual -208 kJ mol^-1 is about 152 kJ mol^-1 less exothermic, so benzene is lower in energy (more stable) than a localised structure.
This extra stability is explained by delocalisation of the pi electrons around the whole ring.
X-ray diffraction: all benzene C-C bonds are 139 pm, whereas cyclohexene has C=C 129 pm and C-C 150 and 153 pm; a Kekule structure would have alternating long and short bonds.
Benzene bond length lies between C=C and C-C and all six are equal, so the pi electrons are shared evenly around the ring, not localised in three double bonds.
Bromination: cyclohexene reacts with bromine at room temperature (electrophilic addition), while benzene needs FeBr3 and heat and gives a substitution product, bromobenzene.
Delocalised electrons make the ring less electron-rich at any one bond and keep the stable ring intact (substitution rather than addition), so benzene does not behave like an alkene.

questions.question: Discuss the evidence, including one example each from spectroscopy, thermochemistry and the type of reaction normally undergone, that supports a delocalised ring of electrons as the better representation of benzene.
questions.answer: Spectroscopy (1H NMR at about 7.3 ppm from a ring current), thermochemistry (hydrogenation about 150 kJ mol-1 less exothermic than 3 x cyclohexene), and reaction type (substitution rather than addition) all support delocalisation
steps: Spectroscopy: in 1H NMR the aromatic H atoms of benzene appear at about 7.3 ppm, which is further downfield than alkene H atoms (about 5-6 ppm).
This shift is due to a ring current from the delocalised pi electrons, which deshields the H atoms.
Thermochemistry: the enthalpy of hydrogenation of benzene is about -208 kJ mol-1, compared with -360 kJ mol-1 for 3 localised C=C bonds.
The difference of about 150 kJ mol-1 is the delocalisation energy, showing benzene is more stable than the cyclic triene.
Reaction type: benzene undergoes electrophilic substitution, keeping the ring, whereas a cyclic triene would undergo addition like an alkene.
Together these show that the delocalised ring is the better representation of benzene.

questions.question: Complete the mechanism, including curly arrows, for the Friedel-Crafts acylation of benzene to phenylethanone (describe the steps in words, as the diagram is shown in the figure below).
questions.answer: The CH3CO+ electrophile is attacked by the benzene pi electrons, forming an arrowed C-C bond and a delocalised arenium cation; a base (AlCl4-) removes H+, restoring the ring and giving phenylethanone
steps: Curly arrow 1: a pi electron pair from the benzene ring moves to form a new C-C bond to the CH3CO+ electrophile.
The ring now has a positive charge delocalised over 5 carbons, the arenium (sigma) intermediate.
Curly arrow 2: a C-H bond electron pair moves back into the ring, removing H+ from the carbon that bears the new acyl group.
AlCl4- takes the H+ to form HCl and regenerate the AlCl3 catalyst, so the aromatic ring is restored and phenylethanone is formed.

questions.question: Write an equation to show how the electrophile CH3CO+ could be generated.
questions.answer: CH3COCl + AlCl3 -> CH3CO+ + AlCl4-
steps: Ethanoyl chloride (CH3COCl) reacts with the Lewis acid catalyst AlCl3.
The Al atom accepts a lone pair from Cl, which breaks the C-Cl bond.
This gives the electrophile CH3CO+ (acylium ion) and the AlCl4- ion.

questions.question: Explain why phenol reacts with bromine more readily than benzene reacts with bromine.
questions.answer: A lone pair on the oxygen of phenol is delocalised into the ring, raising electron density, so the ring is more attractive to bromine and reacts without a catalyst
steps: The O atom of the -OH group has a lone pair that is donated into the benzene ring.
This increases the electron density of the ring, making it more nucleophilic.
Bromine is therefore attacked more readily and no halogen carrier is needed.

questions.question: Complete the flow diagram showing benzene converted into nitrobenzene (the reagents and conditions are the missing parts).
questions.answer: Benzene -> nitrobenzene using concentrated nitric acid and concentrated sulfuric acid (catalyst) at about 50 C
steps: Concentrated HNO3 is mixed with concentrated H2SO4, which protonates HNO3 and generates the NO2+ electrophile.
Benzene is attacked by NO2+ and substitution gives nitrobenzene.
The mixture is warmed to about 50 C to speed up the reaction.

questions.question: Calculate the percentage yield if 0.642 g of nitrobenzene was made from 0.936 g of benzene. Give the answer to an appropriate number of significant figures.
steps: Mr(C6H5NO2) = 123.11, so theoretical mass of nitrobenzene = 0.01198 x 123.11 = 1.475 g (1:1 mole ratio).
Percentage yield = (0.642 / 1.475) x 100 = 43.5 %.
Answer given to 3 significant figures, the same as the data.

questions.question: Explain how the results of X-ray diffraction experiments on benzene suggest a delocalised structure rather than the Kekule structure.
questions.answer: All six C-C bonds in benzene are the same length (about 0.139 nm), intermediate between C-C (0.154 nm) and C=C (0.134 nm), which fits delocalisation rather than alternating single and double bonds
steps: X-ray diffraction measures the distances between atoms.
The Kekule structure predicts alternating long C-C (0.154 nm) and short C=C (0.134 nm) bonds.
The measured C-C bonds in benzene are all equal, at about 0.139 nm.
This intermediate length is consistent with a delocalised ring of electrons, so it supports the delocalised structure.

questions.question: The compound 1,2-dichlorobenzene exists as only one structure. Explain how this supports the delocalised structure of benzene rather than the Kekule structure.
questions.answer: The Kekule structure would give two different 1,2-dichlorobenzene isomers (Cl on a C=C or on a C-C), but only one is found, so the bonds must be equivalent, as in the delocalised structure
steps: In the Kekule structure the two adjacent C atoms may be joined by a double bond or by a single bond.
This would give two different 1,2-dichlorobenzene isomers.
Only one 1,2-dichlorobenzene is observed.
So all C-C bonds must be equivalent, which is the case only for the delocalised structure.

questions.question: State how the enthalpy changes of hydrogenation for cyclohexene and benzene provide evidence for the delocalised structure.
questions.answer: Benzene's enthalpy of hydrogenation (about -208 kJ mol-1) is less exothermic than 3 x cyclohexene (-360 kJ mol-1), showing benzene is more stable by about 150 kJ mol-1, which is delocalisation energy
steps: Cyclohexene: -120 kJ mol-1 per C=C, so 3 x -120 = -360 kJ mol-1 would be expected for a Kekule benzene.
Benzene's actual value is about -208 kJ mol-1, which is less exothermic.
Benzene is therefore more stable by about 150 kJ mol-1 than the localised structure predicts, showing delocalisation.

questions.question: Describe the structure of benzene in terms of the atomic orbitals involved, the bonds formed and the delocalised electrons.
questions.answer: Each C is sp2 hybridised; the sp2 orbitals form sigma C-C and C-H bonds in a planar hexagon, and the unhybridised p orbitals overlap sideways to form a delocalised pi system of 6 electrons above and below the ring
steps: Each carbon atom is sp2 hybridised, with three sp2 orbitals in a plane at 120 degrees.
Sigma bonds form from overlap of sp2 orbitals: six C-C and six C-H bonds, all in one plane.
Each carbon has one unhybridised p orbital at right angles to the ring.
These p orbitals overlap sideways to form a delocalised pi system of 6 electrons, above and below the ring.

questions.question: Evidence for the aromaticity of a ten-carbon ring compound is that the C-C bonds in the ring: A alternate in length between single and double bonds, B all have similar lengths, C have no regular pattern of bond length, D are all similar to the C=C bond length.
questions.answer: B all have similar lengths
steps: Aromatic rings have delocalised electrons, which make all the ring bonds equal in length.
Option A describes an alternating Kekule-type structure, which is not aromatic.
Option C describes an irregular structure and option D describes C=C bonds, which are not consistent with aromaticity.
So the correct answer is B.

questions.question: The aromaticity is due to the formation of pi bonds as a result of overlap of: A s and p orbitals, B p and d orbitals, C p orbitals, D d orbitals.
questions.answer: C p orbitals
steps: Pi bonds form from sideways overlap of p orbitals on adjacent atoms.
The unhybridised p orbitals on each ring carbon overlap to form the delocalised pi system.
s and d orbitals do not form the pi system in an aromatic ring.
So the answer is C, p orbitals.

questions.question: A 2.00 g sample of naphthalene was nitrated to give 2.57 g of 1-nitronaphthalene. What is the percentage yield? A 95.1 %, B 77.8 %, C 74.0 %, D 57.6 %.
steps: 1:1 mole ratio gives theoretical 1-nitronaphthalene, Mr(C10H7NO2) = 173.17, so theoretical mass = 0.01561 x 173.17 = 2.703 g.
Percentage yield = (2.57 / 2.703) x 100 = 95.1 %.

questions.question: A student calculated a percentage yield greater than 100 %. What is the most likely explanation? A there was unreacted naphthalene present, B the naphthalene was impure, C the sample of 1-nitronaphthalene was damp, D other isomers of 1-nitronaphthalene were produced.
questions.answer: C the sample of 1-nitronaphthalene was damp
steps: A yield above 100 % means the measured mass of product is greater than the theoretical mass.
A damp sample contains extra water, which adds to the measured mass.
Other isomers would not add to the mass of 1-nitronaphthalene, and impure starting material would not raise the product mass above theory.
So the most likely cause is a damp product, option C.

questions.question: For C6H5OH + 3Br2 -> C6H2Br3OH + 3HBr, with Mr values C6H5OH 94.0, Br2 159.8, C6H2Br3OH 330.7 and HBr 80.9, what is the percentage atom economy for the formation of 2,4,6-tribromophenol? A 42.3 %, B 57.7 %, C 69.0 %, D 100 %.
steps: Total mass of reactants = 94.0 + 3 x 159.8 = 573.4.
Mass of desired product = 330.7.
Atom economy = 330.7 / 573.4 x 100 = 57.7 %, option B.

questions.question: When 5.00 g of phenol was reacted and purified, the percentage yield of 2,4,6-tribromophenol was 76.8 %. What mass of purified 2,4,6-tribromophenol was formed? A 3.84 g, B 13.5 g, C 17.6 g, D 22.9 g.
steps: 1:1 with tribromophenol gives theoretical mass = 0.05319 x 330.7 = 17.59 g.
Actual mass = 17.59 x 0.768 = 13.5 g, option B.

questions.question: The formation of nitrobenzene requires benzene and concentrated nitric and sulfuric acids. Which is an equation for the reaction that forms the electrophile? The options are shown in the figure below.
questions.answer: B: HNO3 + 2H2SO4 -> NO2+ + 2HSO4- + H3O+
steps: The electrophile is the nitronium ion NO2+, formed when nitric acid accepts protons from sulfuric acid.
B is balanced (5 H, 11 O, one N on each side; charge 0 on each side) and shows HSO4- as the conjugate base of H2SO4 and water leaving as H3O+.
A also balances but forms SO4^2- (ionising H2SO4 twice), which does not happen in concentrated acid; C and D do not give NO2+ or are not sensible equations.

questions.question: Which type of data is NOT used as evidence for the structure or stability of the benzene ring? A infrared spectroscopy, B mass spectrometry, C thermochemical, D X-ray diffraction.
questions.answer: B mass spectrometry
steps: Infrared spectroscopy shows the C-H and ring absorption bands, which give structural evidence.
Thermochemical data (enthalpy of hydrogenation) give stability evidence.
X-ray diffraction gives equal C-C bond lengths, which is structural evidence.
Mass spectrometry gives the molar mass and fragmentation, which does not show ring structure or stability, so it is the answer.

questions.question: The cumene process is the main industrial method for making phenol. What is the atom economy by mass of the cumene process? A 61 %, B 62 %, C 94 %, D 95 %. (The overall equation is C6H6 + C3H6 + O2 -> C6H5OH + CH3COCH3.)
steps: Overall equation: C6H6 + C3H6 + O2 -> C6H5OH + CH3COCH3.
Mass of phenol = 94.11.
Atom economy = 94.11 / 152.19 x 100 = 61.8 %, which rounds to 62 %.

questions.question: Complete the incomplete Hess cycle for benzene by adding balancing numbers (the cycle diagram is shown in the figure below).
questions.answer: 6C(g) + 6H(g) (top left); 6C(s) + 3H2(g) (bottom left)
steps: Top left: benzene has 6 C and 6 H, so atomising it gives 6C(g) + 6H(g).
Bottom left: the elements in their standard states are 6C(s) + 3H2(g) (3 H2 provide 6 H atoms).

questions.topic: Mean C-C Bond Enthalpy in Benzene
questions.question: Calculate the mean carbon-carbon bond enthalpy in benzene using the completed Hess cycle and the data shown in the PDF (the enthalpy data table is shown in the figure below).
questions.answer: +507 kJ mol^-1
steps: Atomisation of the elements: 6 x (+715) + 3 x (+436) = 4290 + 1308 = +5598 kJ mol^-1.
Hess: 5598 = (+49.0) + (+31) + enthalpy of atomisation of C6H6(g), so atomisation of C6H6(g) = 5598 - 80 = +5518 kJ mol^-1.
This breaks 6 C-H bonds (6 x 413 = 2478) and 6 equal C-C bonds: 5518 - 2478 = 3040 kJ mol^-1.
Mean C-C bond enthalpy = 3040 / 6 = +507 kJ mol^-1 (506.7).

questions.question: Explain why the bond enthalpy calculated in (a)(ii) is not the exact mean of the C=C (+612 kJ mol-1) and C-C (+347 kJ mol-1) bond enthalpies expected from the Kekule structure.
questions.answer: The benzene C-C bonds are all equal and intermediate, because the pi electrons are delocalised; this delocalisation makes benzene more stable (lower in energy), so the mean bond enthalpy is not the simple average of single and double bonds
steps: A Kekule structure would have three C=C and three C-C bonds, so the mean would be (612 + 347) / 2 = 479.5 kJ mol-1.
In benzene, the delocalised pi electrons spread over all six bonds, so each C-C bond is stronger than a single bond but weaker than a full double bond.
The extra stability from delocalisation lowers the energy of benzene.
So the calculated mean differs from the simple Kekule average because of delocalisation energy.

questions.question: Describe how all the carbon-carbon bonds in benzene are formed.
questions.answer: Each C-C bond is a sigma bond from overlap of sp2 hybrid orbitals, and the unhybridised p orbitals overlap sideways to form a delocalised pi system over all six carbons
steps: Each C atom is sp2 hybridised, with three sp2 orbitals in a plane.
Adjacent sp2 orbitals overlap end-on to form sigma C-C bonds, six in total in the ring.
Each C also has an unhybridised p orbital at right angles to the ring.
These p orbitals overlap sideways to form a pi system delocalised across all six C atoms.

questions.question: State one chemical property and one physical property of benzene which would not be expected for a compound with the Kekule structure.
questions.answer: Chemical: benzene undergoes substitution rather than addition with bromine (keeps the ring); Physical: all C-C bonds are equal in length (about 0.139 nm), not alternating
steps: Chemical property: a Kekule cyclic triene would decolourise bromine water by addition, but benzene does not, and undergoes substitution instead.
Physical property: a Kekule structure would have alternating C-C (0.154 nm) and C=C (0.134 nm) bond lengths.
Benzene's measured bond lengths are all about 0.139 nm, which the Kekule structure does not predict.

questions.question: Compare and contrast the bromination of benzene and the bromination of phenol. Include equations; detailed mechanisms are not required.
questions.answer: Benzene: C6H6 + Br2 -> C6H5Br + HBr with an AlBr3/FeBr3 catalyst, requiring heat or catalyst; phenol: C6H5OH + 3Br2 -> C6H2Br3OH + 3HBr at room temperature with no catalyst, substituting 2, 4 and 6 positions
steps: Both are electrophilic substitution reactions, in which H on the ring is replaced by Br and HBr is formed.
Benzene: C6H6 + Br2 -> C6H5Br + HBr, using a halogen carrier (AlBr3 or FeBr3) as catalyst.
Phenol: C6H5OH + 3Br2 -> C6H2Br3OH + 3HBr, with no catalyst needed at room temperature.
Phenol's O lone pair is delocalised into the ring, increasing ring electron density, so phenol reacts faster.
Benzene gives a single monobromo product, whereas phenol is substituted at positions 2, 4 and 6 by excess bromine.
The benzene ring is stable and resists addition, whereas the activated phenol ring is more reactive.
